about.title: About DiGRA South Africa
about.text:
DiGRA South Africa is the official South African chapter of the Digital Games Research Association — the world's largest academic organisation dedicated to the study of digital games.

We exist to grow game studies in Africa. That means building research capacity, connecting scholars across the continent, and making sure African perspectives reach international journals, conferences, and conversations.

gap.title: African Games. African Scholarship.
gap.text:
Global game studies has a blind spot. The canonical texts treat Western, Japanese, and North American game cultures as defaults — as if games exist outside of geography and history.

South African game culture is distinct: shaped by post-apartheid demographics, mobile-first access patterns, a growing independent development industry, and rich indigenous play traditions that predate digital games entirely.

who.title: The South African Chapter
who.text:
DiGRA South Africa is the official South African regional chapter of the Digital Games Research Association (DiGRA) International — the world's leading academic organisation dedicated to the study of digital games (founded 2003).

DiGRA International has formally accepted the establishment of the DiGRA South Africa Chapter. As a regional chapter, DiGRA SA operates within DiGRA International's framework while addressing South African and African priorities in research, policy, industry partnerships, and community development.

mission.title: Mission & Goals
mission.text: To establish a sustainable, coherent, and collaborative national ecosystem for game studies, game research, and game-related academic activity across South Africa and the African continent.

goals.title: Build national academic legitimacy for game studies
goals.text: Publish peer-reviewed research on African games — from cultural analysis to game design theory — in international venues.

goals.title: Strengthen local and regional research networks
goals.text: Train the next generation of African game scholars through mentorship, workshops, and access to DiGRA International resources.

goals.title: Connect academia with industry and professional practice
goals.text: Link game researchers across South Africa and the continent into a working network — not just a mailing list.

goals.title: Promote African scholarship in global DiGRA spaces
goals.text: Get African voices into DiGRA International conferences, panels, and publications on an ongoing basis.

aims.title: What We're Here to Do
aims.text: The chapter has a specific mandate: build the infrastructure for game studies to flourish in Africa. These are the concrete aims that guide everything we do.

field.title: Game Studies in South Africa
field.text:
Game studies as a discipline has grown significantly since the early 2000s — but African contexts have been systematically underrepresented in international scholarship. Most canonical game studies texts treat Western, Japanese, and North American game cultures as the default.

South African game culture is distinct: shaped by post-apartheid demographics, mobile-first access patterns, a small but active development industry, and rich indigenous game traditions that predate digital games entirely.

DiGRA SA exists to produce, publish, and disseminate research that takes this context seriously.

asides.title: Did You Know?
asides.text: South Africa has one of the most active independent game development scenes on the continent, with dedicated studios in Cape Town, Johannesburg, and Pretoria.

asides.title: Our Approach
asides.text: We apply African philosophy, ubuntu principles, and decolonial methodology to game research — not as a critique of existing work, but as an expansion of it.

library.title: DiGRA Digital Library
library.text:
The DiGRA Digital Library hosts thousands of conference papers, journal articles, and proceedings — all freely accessible. It's one of the largest open-access repositories in game studies.

As a DiGRA SA member, you gain direct pathways to contribute to the library through DiGRA International conferences and publications.

team.name: Amanda Jankowitz
team.bio: Amanda Jankowitz is a Lecturer at the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. She specialises in game-based learning, immersive simulation, and ethical AI integration, exploring how playful, technology-enhanced pedagogy can advance engagement, equity, and educator development in healthcare education.

team.name: Dr Olu Randle
team.bio: Dr Olu Randle is a digital arts academic and lead researcher of the Games Artificial Intelligence and Culture (GAIC) Lab at the University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa. He specialises in game design, machine intelligence, and computational creativity, with a focus on applying artificial intelligence to African board games, digital culture, and indigenous language technologies to advance innovation and access within 4IR contexts.

team.name: Bernice Beukes
team.bio: Bernice Beukes is a higher education educator with over 15 years of teaching experience. She specialises in accounting education and technology‑enhanced learning, with a focus on innovative pedagogical practices that integrate both emerging and established technologies to enhance student learning; her work has been recognised with an Education Innovation Award in 2017.

team.name: Dr Andrea Hayes
team.bio: Dr Andrea Hayes is a Game Design lecturer at the Digital Arts Department at Wits University. Her research areas in game studies include gender in video games, queer games and how video games intersect with the Anthropocene.

team.name: Prof Veruschka Pelser-Carstens
team.bio: Prof Veruschka Pelser-Carstens is an Associate Professor in the School of Accounting Sciences at North-West University (NWU), South Africa. She holds a PhD from the University of Joensuu, Finland, and has over 20 years of experience in higher education. Her research focuses on accountancy education, with a particular emphasis on serious games, game-based learning, and innovative pedagogical approaches to enhance student engagement and learning outcomes. Her publications are centred on serious games and accountancy education, contributing to the advancement of teaching and learning within the discipline. Prof Pelser-Carstens has received multiple teaching excellence awards in recognition of her commitment to student-centred learning and pedagogical innovation.

team.name: Dr Anusia Govender-Elshove
team.bio: Dr. Anusia Govender-Elshove is the daughter of her pioneering Indian Classical dancer mother and aunt (South Africa, 1961). With interests in interweaving Indo-Afro-Asian culture, her research explores decolonial methodologies through family archives. She is also a game creator exploring Indian indenture, migration and South African diasporic histories and issues through interactive, Real-world games used in an educational, narrative as well as curatorial manner.

team.name: Dr Lance Bunt
team.bio: Dr Lance Bunt is a Senior Lecturer at North-West University, South Africa. He specialises in gameful learning, serious game design, and technology enhanced pedagogy. His work explores player experience, instructional design, and systems thinking to improve higher education practice, integrating AI and playful approaches to support meaningful learning.

team.name: Dr Rachel van der Merwe
team.institution: University of Groningen / University of the Free State
team.bio: Rachel is an assistant professor of media studies at the Centre for Media and Journalism Studies at the University of Groningen and a Research Fellow at the Centre for Gender and Africa Studies at the University of the Free State. Her current research project, Gaming the Nation, is a qualitative study of the South African video game industry, which includes an investigation into the role games play in facilitating national and cultural identities.

team.name: Kyle Smith
team.bio: Head of Game Design and Development at Emeris Vega School. My research and professional interests focus on game design, play, and game‑based learning that challenge convention. I am interested in the use of games as tools for meaningful impact, experimentation, and boundary‑pushing creativity across education, culture, and interactive media.

team.name: Angus Davidson
team.bio: Mr Angus Davidson having worked in the IT Development Industry for Internet Solutions and subsequently Dimension Data joined Prof Christo Doherty to create the Digital Arts Department in 2003. He has been the tech leader and the person who has guided the department from the original 20 Student to the nearly 400 it has today.

news.title: Who Makes the Rules? Talking Games at SACOMM 2026
news.author: Dr Andrea Hayes and Dr Lance Bunt
news.image_alt: DiGRA South Africa panellists standing in front of a projected DiGRA SA slide at SACOMM 2026
news.excerpt: How much of an ordinary day already feels like a game? A recap of the DiGRA South Africa panel at SACOMM 2026, from ludification to what makes a game South African.

body.text: Your fitness app wants you to close a ring. Your language app wants you to save your streak. Somewhere, a leaderboard is waiting to tell you that you came fourth at something you didn't realise was a competition. How much of an ordinary day already feels like a game?

That question was our way into the DiGRA South Africa panel at SACOMM 2026, hosted at Wits University. Over 90 minutes, our facilitator, Dr Andrea Hayes, and panellists Vuyo Tswago, Amanda Jankowitz and Dr Lance Bunt took the conversation from the game-like systems we use every day to the challenges of making games in South Africa and getting them seen. For us, as the South African chapter of the Digital Games Research Association, it was a chance to bring game studies into conversation with people thinking about media, communication and culture from all sorts of angles.
You've unlocked a new question

We started with ludification, a wonderfully academic word for the way play and game-like systems seep into everyday life. Gamification is one way that happens. Think of a streak that nudges you to practise every day. Learning through a game can work differently. A simulation might let you make a choice, see what happens and try again. Both approaches give us a practical question to ask in education and health. What can someone actually learn or do here that would be harder to achieve another way?

Thinking like a game designer also changes how you look at platforms. What does the interface reward? What choices does it give you? If the app celebrates you for showing up every day, does it care what you do when you get there? Once you start looking for the rules, a surprising number of apps start to look like games whose designers forgot to hand out the rulebook.
So, what makes a game South African?

Imagine a team in South Africa makes a game about a spaceship. The crew speaks English, the setting is a distant galaxy and the intended audience lives everywhere. Is it a South African game? Would your answer change if the crew spoke isiZulu? And what happens when developers feel they have to make their work recognisably South African before it gets counted as such?

That question has a different bite when a game is built for a particular classroom or health setting. There, language, humour and familiar situations can shape whether the people it was made for can use it. A studio making a commercial game might face a different pressure altogether. How much of a story do you explain for an international audience, and how much do you trust players to figure out as they go?
Great, you made a game. Can anyone find it?

Getting a game onto Steam, PlayStation or even a mobile app store is one milestone. Getting it in front of someone who might love it is another. Search, recommendations and storefront placement can shape what people discover. That leaves game development programmes with a practical question. Alongside teaching students how to make a game, how can universities prepare them for the work of finding an audience and building a career?

Even the way we count success could use a rethink. A player might spend dozens of hours in an international release without realising that South African developers helped build, illustrate or test it. If we look only for games released under a local studio's name, how much of the work happening here slips out of view?
We saved some time for audience questions and ended with a fill-in-the-blank prompt that's harder than it looks. If you had to pick just one thing, what would you put in the space?
The South African games industry needs more ________.

news.title: DiGRA South Africa Board Updates and Call for Nominations
news.excerpt: We're inviting nominations for two Student Representatives, one Industry Representative and a Secretary. Nominations and self-nominations close on 31 January 2027.

body.text: DiGRA South Africa continues to grow as a vibrant community of researchers, educators, students, developers, and industry professionals interested in games, play, and interactive media. As our chapter expands its activities and prepares for future initiatives, we are inviting nominations to fill several vacancies on the Board.
These appointments will help ensure that the Board remains representative of the diverse communities that contribute to game studies and games-related practice across South Africa.
Current Board vacancies
Nominations are invited for:

Two Student Representative positions (undergraduate and/or postgraduate students)
One Industry Representative position
One Secretary position
We particularly encourage nominations from individuals who can bring diverse perspectives, experiences, disciplines, institutions, regions, and career stages to the chapter's leadership.
Who can be nominated?
Suitable nominees may include:

Undergraduate or postgraduate students with an interest in game studies, game-based learning, game development, esports, interactive media, or related fields.
Industry professionals working in game development, design, esports, educational technology, serious games, or related sectors.
Community members who are passionate about supporting the growth and sustainability of DiGRA South Africa.
Both nominations and self-nominations are welcome.
Nomination process
To submit a nomination, please provide:

The nominee's name
Current affiliation or organisation
A short biography
A brief motivation for the nomination
Confirmation that the nominee is willing to serve if appointed
Nominations close on 31 January 2027.
Should more than one nomination be received for a position, a Board vote will be conducted in accordance with the chapter's governance processes.
Interested in getting involved?

If you are interested in serving on the DiGRA South Africa Board, or would like to learn more about any of the available positions, we encourage you to contact any current Board member for an informal discussion. Board members will be happy to answer questions about the roles, responsibilities, and opportunities associated with serving on the chapter's leadership team.
Growing our community

The continued growth of DiGRA South Africa depends on the energy and contributions of its members. By bringing new voices and perspectives into leadership, we can continue building an inclusive, collaborative, and impactful community that supports games scholarship, teaching, research, and industry engagement across the region.
We look forward to welcoming new Board members and working together to shape the future of DiGRA South Africa.
Interested candidates can contact any DiGRA South Africa Board member before the closing date of 31 January 2027 to express their interest or discuss nomination opportunities.

body.text: DiGRA SA officially launched on 2 June 2026 at 18:00 (SAST) with an online panel discussion titled: Why Games Matter Here: Digital Games Research in South Africa and the Global South.

The launch panel brought together diverse voices to reflect on the relevance, impact, and future of digital games research in South Africa and across the Global South, spanning academia, industry, education, culture, and policy.
DiGRA founding members and invited guests explored why games research matters here, and how local and Global South perspectives can contribute to and reshape global conversations in the field.

news.title: Announcing DiGRA South Africa
news.excerpt: Introducing DiGRA South Africa: the official South African chapter of the Digital Games Research Association, building a home for game studies across the continent.

body.text: We are proud to announce the launch of DiGRA South Africa (DiGRA SA), the official South African chapter of the Digital Games Research Association (DiGRA).

DiGRA SA has been established to build and connect a vibrant, sustainable ecosystem for game studies, game research, and game-related academic activity across South Africa and the African continent. As part of the international DiGRA network, the chapter creates a home for scholars, educators, students, designers, and industry partners interested in the study and practice of games and play.
Why DiGRA South Africa?
Game studies has grown rapidly worldwide, yet African perspectives, contexts, and research remain underrepresented in global conversations. DiGRA SA exists to change that by:

Supporting research on games, play, and game cultures rooted in African contexts
Connecting academia, industry, and creative practice
Creating pathways for students and early-career researchers into international scholarship
Hosting events, workshops, symposia, and game-related activities
Amplifying African voices within global game studies networks
What's next?
2026 marks DiGRA SA's founding year. Over the coming months we will be rolling out:

A series of webinars and academic events
Opportunities to become founding members
Calls for participation in research, games, and special interest groups
Formal announcements about membership, governance, and programmes
We invite researchers, students, educators, developers, and practitioners from South Africa and across the continent to join us in shaping the future of game studies in and from Africa.
Stay connected: follow our updates, attend our upcoming events, and be part of this growing community.
